results.title: SaladCloud Recipes: Deploy Faster on Distributed GPUs
results.author: Maksim Gorkii
highlights:
Learn how SaladCloud recipes simplify distributed GPU deployment with tested defaults, reusable templates, and ready-to-run configurations.

Maksim Gorkii

SaladCloud Tutorials Thu Aug 20 2026

SaladCloud recipes are designed to remove friction for teams that want to ship quickly on distributed infrastructure. Each recipe bundles best-practice configurations, tested defaults, and concrete operational guidance so that operators can stay focused on business logic instead of infrastructure plumbing.

...

Each recipe is designed around how SaladCloud expects workloads to be deployed and managed, including configuration such as health probes where appropriate. Once your Container Group is running, you can use the Portal to monitor its status, inspect logs, edit the deployment, and scale replicas just like any other workload.

Another important aspect of usability is how recipes interact with cost. There is no separate billing surface for recipes. Once deployed, they are billed exactly like any other Salad Container Group: based on the amount of time your workload replicas are running. SaladCloud Documentation

That simplicity lets teams experiment with recipes during early validation without worrying about a separate pricing model. If you already understand how SaladCloud charges for Container Groups, you already understand how recipes show up on your bill.

results.title: RNP-023 Milestone 3: Bringing Salad's Payment Rails On-Chain
results.author: Bob Miles
highlights:
Bringing Salad's Payment Rails On-Chain: Our Milestone 3 Architecture

# Bringing Salad's Payment Rails On-Chain: Our Milestone 3 Architecture

Salad's implementation design for RNP-023 Milestone 3: x402 batch settlement, daily on-chain burns, and RENDER Chef rewards.

Bob Miles

SaladCloud Tue Aug 11 2026

By Bob Miles (Co-founder & CEO), Kyle Dodson (CTO) & Cory Rieth (Head of Product)

Milestones 1 and 2 of RNP-023 are live: Chefs can take rewards in RENDER, and customers can fund their accounts with it. Milestone 3 is the big one: moving Salad's payment rails onto the Render Network's burn-mint-equilibrium model. Here's the design we're building, in the open, while it's still cheap to change.

When the Render community approved RNP-023, Salad committed to becoming a Render Network subnet and migrating our compute marketplace, SaladCloud's container engine (SCE) and gateway service (SGS), onto RENDER as the transactional layer. Milestone 1 (RENDER rewards for Chefs) and Milestone 2 (RENDER deposits for customers) shipped on schedule. Milestone 3 moves the rails themselves: every transaction flowing through the burn-mint-equilibrium (BME) model, with burns, fees, and rewards visible on-chain.

This post is the implementation design for that milestone. We're publishing it before we finish building for the same reason the RNP process exists: so the Render Foundation and community can kick the tires while the design is still cheap to change. Everything here implements RNP-023 as written: the same revenue splits, the same burn model, the same pricing source. What's new is how we deliver it. Since Milestones 1 and 2 shipped, we've redesigned the crypto payment path around x402 batch settlement, an open standard that fits this problem almost exactly, and built a settlement engine with one job: making every number on the dashboard provably correct. We've workshopped the approach with the Render Foundation along the way; now we want the community's eyes on it.

...

GPU ... into

...

The Milestone 3 target architecture: existing platform unchanged, one new settlement engine, and a small set of on-chain wallets for escrows, burns, fees, and Chef rewards.

...

## Following the value Copy Anchor Link

RNP-023 defines how revenue splits between burns, the Render Foundation's protocol administration fee, and Salad as the network operator:

| Product | Burned | Render Foundation | Salad |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Salad Container Engine (SCE) | 60% | 5% | 35% |
| Salad Gateway Service (SGS) | 35% | 5% | 60% |

The interesting question is how value travels from a customer's payment to those splits. The answer differs by rail, and the crypto rail is where the design has changed most since Milestone 2.

...

When a customer pays in RENDER, their RENDER doesn't transfer to Salad. They go into the customer's own on-chain settlement account: an escrow governed by x402 batch settlement, the open HTTP-native payment standard's scheme for exactly this shape of problem: deposit once, meter usage off-chain, settle on-chain in batches. Three rules govern the account:

1. Salad can draw only what you've consumed. Our drafting rights are capped by metered usage, and usage is throttled against your remaining escrow balance (with a safety buffer for price moves), so an account can't overrun between settlements.
2. We draw once a day. At each epoch close, we draft exactly the day's consumption, converted from USD at the same 24-hour TWAP used everywhere else in the system, into our Receipts wallet, and the burn splits execute from there the same day.
3. Unused RENDER stays yours. After the predefined settlement window, you can withdraw whatever we haven't drawn: self-serve, on-chain, no support ticket. Refunds stop being a policy and become a property of the contract.

...

On the supply side, Chefs accrue earnings in USD as work completes, and those accruals convert to RENDER at the close of each daily epoch using the 24-hour TWAP from Jupiter that the RNP mandates. That's the same price, in the same epoch, as the burns. We'll walk that path in the Chef section below.

...

Once a day, the settlement engine closes the books:

The daily settlement sequence. Burns and Chef rewards settle in the same epoch, at the same 24h TWAP, and a paused epoch settles late rather than wrong.

One design choice here matters more than it looks: burns and Chef rewards settle in the same epoch, at the same 24-hour TWAP. That makes "RENDER burned vs. RENDER emitted" an exact daily comparison rather than an approximation across different timestamps and prices: one pair of numbers, published every day, each side traceable to its transactions.

That comparison is the heart of RNP-023's economics. The model is built so that burns exceed the emissions that fund Chef rewards, structurally, by burning 4% of revenue over and above what Chefs earn. We're designing this integration to deliver on that intent, and we want to be equally clear about the honest caveat: the differential is structural, not guaranteed per-epoch. Because burns and emissions are priced when they settle, sharp moves in RENDER's price between epochs can compress the gap in some periods and widen it in others. The RNP's own worked examples show the spread ranging from roughly 2% to 18% depending on price path. Two things keep this honest over time: the monthly top-up burn the RNP requires, which trues up aggregate burns against actual margins, and the daily public numbers, which let anyone audit the cumulative ratio rather than taking our word for it.

One more expectation to set: the burn line will not be a smooth curve, and it shouldn't be. Daily burns track daily consumption, which already varies meaningfully: customers scale up and down, hardware mixes shift, workloads come and go. On top of that you'll see the monthly SGS settlement spike, occasional one-time burns from large prepaid contracts, and, if our price cross-check ever diverges, an epoch that settles late at the next good price. We'd rather explain a gap than defend a bad number.

...

This post describes Salad's current engineering design for RNP-023 Milestone 3. It is shared for community feedback, not as a finalized specification; details, including settlement windows, epoch mechanics, reward mechanics, and provider choices, may change as we iterate with the Render Foundation and community and complete legal and operational review. Figures from RNP-023 are illustrative.
